subject: english
title: KS3 English diagnostic
curriculum: National Curriculum in England, key stage 3 English programme of study (2013)

skills.name: Finding information
skills.why: Finding the right details quickly is the first step in understanding any text.
skills.strong: {name} reads carefully and picks out exactly the right details.
skills.developing: {name} finds most details but can miss one when reading quickly.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet finding details in a text reliably. Every reading task depends on this, so it comes first.
skills.next_step: We will practise close reading and checking answers against the text.

skills.name: Inference and understanding
skills.why: Reading between the lines is what turns a good reader into a strong one, and it is central to GCSE.
skills.strong: {name} reads between the lines well and understands a writer's tone and message.
skills.developing: {name} understands what happens but finds it harder to work out what is suggested.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident working out what a text suggests. This is a key skill for GCSE, so it is worth building now.
skills.next_step: We will talk through small details and what they tell us, building confidence step by step.

skills.name: Language and structure
skills.why: Noticing how writers use words and organise texts helps students both read and write better.
skills.strong: {name} spots writers' techniques and explains their effects well.
skills.developing: {name} can name some techniques but is less sure explaining why a writer uses them.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident explaining how writers use language. This is at the heart of GCSE English, so it is worth starting now.
skills.next_step: We will use short extracts to practise spotting techniques and explaining their effect.

skills.name: Writing and accuracy
skills.why: Clear, accurate writing matters in every subject, not just English.
skills.strong: {name} writes clearly and accurately, with good control of sentences.
skills.developing: {name} has good ideas but makes some errors with punctuation and grammar.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet writing accurately and with control. This affects work in every subject, so it is worth real focus.
skills.next_step: We will practise punctuation and sentence control alongside planning short pieces of writing.

passages.title: The Allotment
passages.text:
Every Saturday morning, my grandad and I walk to his allotment at the edge of town. It takes twenty minutes, and he spends every one of them telling me the names of the birds we pass: robin, blackbird, wren. I never remember them, but I like the way he says them, slowly, as if each one is a small gift.

The allotment itself is not much to look at. It is a long, narrow strip of earth with a shed that leans to one side like a tired old man. Inside the shed there are seven spades, although Grandad only ever uses one.

Last spring we planted potatoes, beans and a row of sunflowers. The potatoes did well and the beans did brilliantly, but the sunflowers were a disaster. Slugs ate every single one before it grew taller than my hand. Grandad just laughed. "That's gardening," he said. "You win some, the slugs win some."

This year I am in charge of the sunflowers. I have read three books about slugs. I have a plan. The slugs, I suspect, also have a plan.

What I have learned from the allotment is not really about vegetables. It is about patience: about putting something small into the ground and trusting that, with enough care, it will grow.

questions.stem: How many minutes does the walk to the allotment take?
questions.explain: Paragraph 1: 'It takes twenty minutes'.

questions.stem:
'a shed that leans to one side like a tired old man'

Which technique is used here?
questions.explain: A comparison using 'like' is a simile.

questions.stem: On which day do they go to the allotment?
questions.explain: 'Every Saturday morning'.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.explain: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. 'park' is not a proper noun here.

questions.stem: Which TWO crops grew well last spring?
questions.explain: 'The potatoes did well and the beans did brilliantly, but the sunflowers were a disaster.'

questions.stem: How does the narrator feel about Grandad telling them the names of the birds?
questions.explain: 'I like the way he says them' shows enjoyment, even though they never remember the names.

questions.stem:
'the beans did brilliantly'

Which word in this phrase is an adverb?
questions.explain: 'Brilliantly' describes how the beans did, so it is an adverb.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling?
questions.explain: Because.

questions.stem: What happened to the sunflowers last spring?
options: Slugs ate them before they grew taller than the narrator's hand
questions.explain: 'Slugs ate every single one before it grew taller than my hand.'

questions.stem: When the sunflowers fail, 'Grandad just laughed.' What does this show about him?
options: He is relaxed and does not let setbacks upset him
He did not care about the garden
He was glad the sunflowers died
He had not noticed what happened
questions.explain: 'You win some, the slugs win some' shows a calm, good-humoured attitude to failure.

questions.stem: The writer lists the birds: 'robin, blackbird, wren'. What is the effect of this list?
options: It shows the narrator is bored
It explains how to look after birds
It helps the reader picture a walk full of nature
questions.explain: Naming specific birds builds a vivid picture of the walk.

questions.stem:
'This year I am in charge of the sunflowers. I have read three books about slugs. I have a plan.'

What does this suggest about the narrator?
options: They are determined to succeed this year
They want to give up gardening
questions.explain: Reading three books and making a plan shows determination.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
options: I bought apples, pears, and, grapes.
I bought apples pears, and grapes.
I bought apples, pears and grapes.
I, bought apples pears and grapes.
questions.explain: Commas separate items in a list; no comma is needed after 'and' or after the subject.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is NOT true, according to the text?
options: The narrator always remembers the names of the birds
The shed leans to one side
Grandad only ever uses one spade
The narrator has read three books about slugs
questions.explain: 'I never remember them.' The other three are stated in the text.

questions.stem:
'The slugs, I suspect, also have a plan.'

What is the tone of this sentence?
questions.explain: Imagining slugs making plans is playful and funny.

questions.stem: Why does the writer use very short sentences in 'I have read three books about slugs. I have a plan.'?
options: To show the narrator cannot write well
To build a sense of determination, with a comic touch
To slow down a sad moment
questions.explain: Short, punchy sentences sound determined, and they set up the joke that follows.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written in the passive voice?
options: The sunflowers were eaten by the slugs.
questions.explain: In the passive voice the thing acted on comes first: 'The sunflowers were eaten by the slugs.'

questions.stem: Why might the writer end with a paragraph about patience rather than about vegetables?
options: To show the allotment matters more for what it teaches than for what it grows
To prove the vegetables were a failure
To give instructions for planting potatoes
To show they are bored of the allotment
questions.explain: The ending widens the meaning: the allotment is really about learning patience.

questions.stem: How is the text organised?
options: As a description of one single moment
It moves from describing the allotment, to a story about last year, to what the writer has learned
questions.explain: Description, then a past event, then this year, then reflection.

questions.stem:
Write a short paragraph (4 to 6 sentences) describing a place that is special to you.

Help the reader picture it, and explain why it matters to you. Spend about 6 minutes on this.

rubric.criterion: Clear description, using at least one sense or a well-chosen detail
Explains why the place matters to the writer
Varied sentences (not all starting the same way)
Accurate spelling and punctuation, with sentences correctly marked by capital letters and full stops

questions.explain: One mark per strand. Be generous with ideas and strict with sentence punctuation.
